articles.title: "Do you just expect black men to be patriotic?" - Footage of Jokic during the national anthem shows a double standard in the backlash LeBron got
articles.summary: LeBron James faced heavy criticism over his national anthem actions, but Nikola Jokic's footage has added another layer to the debate.
articles.body:
LeBron James is caught in a hurricane after his actions during the national anthem before the Philadelphia 76ers played the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night. Even President Donald Trump weighed in on the controversy after the four-time NBA champion was seen stretching his arms, imitating a golf swing, and taking practice shots.

Trump shared a video of the incident on Truth Social, calling LeBron James a " total disgrace " and demanding an apology to American service members who lost their lives defending the country. He also returned to the issue during a rally in Iowa on Thursday, questioning LeBron's conduct again.

However, LeBron didn't seem interested in taking the bait. After the Sixers' 114-106 comeback win over the Cavs, he gave a short and sly response to the backlash.

"Yeah, it must have been a slow news day at the office," LeBron said .

Jokic comes under fire after similar footage surfaces

Denver Nuggets ' star Nikola Jokic was seen stretching alongside Jamal Murray during the national anthem before the team's Thursday night game against the Oklahoma City Thunder. The three-time league MVP's actions looked similar to LeBron's, but there was no social media backlash for the same.

One X user called out those who had criticized the Ohio native, questioning whether the same standards applied to everyone in the NBA.

"To everyone who had a problem with LeBron James during the national anthem, make sure you go after Jokic as well for literally doing the same thing! Or do you just expect Black men to be patriotic?" the user wrote .

Double standard or incomparable situations?

Still, not everyone agreed with the comparison between the two incidents. Some pointed out that Jokic is Serbian, arguing that nationality matters when discussing patriotism and the national anthem. Others pointed out that stretching during an approximately two-minute anthem was disrespectful regardless of nationality.

Jokic plays in the same league, in the same country, and was seen doing something similar to LeBron. And that raised a fair question — when the national anthem is playing, is it really too much to stand still for a few minutes out of respect?

The warmups are already over, and the game is about to begin. If the backlash is truly about respecting the national anthem, the difference in how LeBron and Nikola were treated was always going to raise eyebrows.

articles.title: How did Jaylen Brown step up without LeBron James? Philadelphia 76ers extend unbeaten start against Milwaukee Bucks
articles.summary: Jaylen Brown turned 30 on October 24, 2026, and gave the Philadelphia 76ers another reason to celebrate.
articles.body: Jaylen Brown turned 30 on October 24, 2026, and gave the Philadelphia 76ers another reason to celebrate. With LeBron James sitting out their game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Brown took on a bigger scoring role and finished with 27 points. Philadelphia won 127-116 to improve to 3-0 in the 2026-27 NBA season.Brown's performance came alongside a big night from Joel Embiid, who recorded a triple-double. The Sixers had enough scoring options to handle James' absence and keep their unbeaten start going. Jaylen Brown takes charge as Philadelphia beats MilwaukeeBrown gave Philadelphia the scoring boost it needed without James. He attacked defenders in the mid-range, used his strength to create room for jump shots and found ways to finish near the basket. He also connected from three-point range, making it difficult for Milwaukee to settle into a defensive rhythm.The 76ers did not need Brown to carry the entire offense. Tyrese Maxey scored 26 points and added four assists, while VJ Edgecombe finished with 17 points and 12 rebounds. Their contributions helped Philadelphia maintain its offensive pressure throughout the game.James sat out because of lower back pain management, according to the Associated Press. The 41-year-old had averaged 15.5 points and 9.5 rebounds in his first two games with Philadelphia. The team had won both contests, beating the New York Knicks and Cleveland Cavaliers.His absence gave Brown more opportunities to create his own shots. Brown's ability to score without needing a pass to set him up offered Philadelphia another option when Milwaukee tried to disrupt its offense.The Bucks still made the Sixers work for the win. Philadelphia had some uneven stretches, but its three-point shooting improved after the team shot below 30% from beyond the arc in each of its first two games. Brown helped keep the offense moving as the Sixers worked to close out the contest.Joel Embiid's triple-double helps the Sixers reach 3-0While Brown led the scoring story, Embiid controlled much of Philadelphia's offense. He finished with 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists, recording the 10th triple-double of his NBA career.Embiid scored in the post and created opportunities for teammates when Milwaukee sent extra defenders his way. His passing helped Brown and Maxey find room to attack, giving Philadelphia more ways to punish the Bucks' defense.Edgecombe also made an early impact with three three-pointers. Foul trouble limited his playing time, but his rebounding added another dimension to his performance. He also helped create a key second-chance opportunity for Embiid late in the game.Dean Wade made his Sixers debut after missing the first two games with an ankle sprain. He hit a corner three-pointer on his first touch and finished with two three-pointers and three steals. His defensive work gave head coach Nick Nurse another useful option.Kentavious Caldwell-Pope added 12 points off the bench and made several important defensive plays. Jabari Walker also contributed on the glass before leaving the game with an injury.Philadelphia's 127-116 victory moved it to 3-0 after wins over the Knicks, Cavaliers and Bucks. The result also gave the team a positive start to a demanding weekend schedule.The Sixers will host the Detroit Pistons on October 25, the second game of their back-to-back. James had already indicated that he would play in only one of the two games that weekend. After beating Milwaukee without him, Philadelphia will look to carry its winning start into the next matchup.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kiah Stokes' historic defensive run continues as Valkyries tie up WNBA Finals
articles.summary: Stokes became the first player in WNBA Finals history to log at least three blocks in four straight games.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Quite a few things needed to change for the Golden State Valkyries if they wanted to notch things up against the Atlanta Dream in Game 4 of the WNBA Finals.

They needed a better version of Gabby Williams, particularly on the offensive end, than they'd gotten in the prior two contests. They needed a more aggressive version of Veronica Burton, one much closer to the regular-season version.

Broadly speaking, they needed more collective energy and focus — a pair of areas that, per head coach Natalie Nakase, the team had shown "uncharacteristic" slippage in.

On Saturday, they got more from Williams, who scored a team-high 17 points and defended at a high level (including three steals). Burton added a series-high 13 points, ramping up her driving volume while also flying around defensively (three steals, two blocks).

The Valkyries even tweaked their rotation: they swapped out Cecilia Zandalasini and Kayla Thornton for Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles in the starting lineup, and, aside from a combined 4:26 from Janelle Salaün (2:34) and Kaitlyn Chen (1:52), generally rolled with a seven-player rotation on their way to the series-tying 67-62 win

If there was a constant, something that didn't need changing, it was the steady play of Kiah Stokes.

Her role is simple: screen hard, connect possessions when asked, clean up the glass on both ends, and eliminate the paint as a scoring option when on the floor.

In Game 4, she once again came to play: 4 points, a playoff career-high 16 rebounds (overall career-high 8 OREB) and 3 air-draining blocks.

History was made with Stokes' third block, a two-handed swat on a DeWanna Bonner drive. She became the first player in WNBA Finals history to log at least three blocks in four straight games. Zooming out, she surpassed a pair of legends in Sylvia Fowles and Brittney Griner for the most total blocks in a Finals series.

This could be enough of a story, Stokes' rim protection in the highest-stakes portion of the season. But what this is, dearest reader, is a continuation of season-long dominance. A kind reminder that she was officially named to this year's All-Defensive Second Team — she'd have made my first team if I had a ballot — just last week for her role on a historically great Valkyries defense.

If we want to narrow things to the postseason, I hope people understand how nuts (complimentary) this run has been for Stokes.

The Valkyries have faced the fifth- (Wings), second- (Aces) and fourth- (Dream) ranked offenses in the league. All three feature All-Star bigs: a playmaking post hub in Jessica Shepard, the literal GOAT in A'ja Wilson, and an ascending superstar in Angel Reese. Three distinct styles of attack.

None of them have had a good time against Stokes.

The Wings series was a fun one; partly Stokes shutting down post touches and drives, partly Stokes acting as a roamer while Thornton defended Shepard's perimeter touches.

Things shifted in Las Vegas, Stokes' old stomping grounds, with the Aces working to move Wilson around the board. There were cross screens to navigate, pindowns to track, pick-and-rolls to defend — and, more often than usual, a healthy dose of switching as part of the diet.

In the Finals, it's been a little bit of everything for Reese. Some low-post touches, some above-the-break hub work, transition attacks, free-throw area flashes to set up attacks, pick-and-roll play.

Stokes, more than any other defender on the Valkyries by a wide margin, has been game for it.

That is not an exaggeration, by the way. Per Second Spectrum, here is how Reese has fared on shots contested by Stokes, compared to the other Valkyries:

And here is how that's played out for those All-Star bigs for the entire postseason:

Shepard: 3-of-12 (25% FG) vs. Stokes; 5-of-11 (45.5% FG) vs. everyone else

Wilson: 10-of-32 (31.3% FG) vs. Stokes; 44-of-72 (61.1% FG) vs. everyone else

Reese: 5-of-21 (23.8% FG) vs. Stokes; 48-of-97 (49.5% FG) vs. everyone else

Total: 18-of-65 (27.7% FG) vs. Stokes; 97-of-180 (53.9% FG) vs. everyone else

Of course, those are just contest numbers. As mentioned earlier, Stokes' work in pick-and-roll has been equal parts impressive and impactful.

Between her length, understanding of angles, willingness to chew up space, and increased comfort as a late-switch option, the Dream haven't had much fun with her. And of course, having stout perimeter defenders like Burton and Williams in front of her relieves pressure.

In Game 4, the Dream generated only 0.58 PPP on trips featuring a ball screen defended by Stokes. That's actually an improvement from Game 3 (13 picks, 0.36 PPP). In fact, it's been fascinating to watch Atlanta's pick-and-roll volume ebb and flow throughout the series — and how Stokes has become less involved as things have gone on. To that end:

Yes, you read correctly: that's 29 picks defended in Game 2, 27 combined in Game 3 and 4.

Zoom out for the entire postseason, and teams have generated only 0.75 PPP on trips featuring a ball screen defended by Stokes — a slightly stingier figure than what was allowed during the regular season (0.76 PPP, second among 45 players to defend at least 300).

The defensive glass work is quieter but, again, incredibly important. Stokes grabbed eight today, and is averaging 7.5 for the series. It's an impressive feat considering Reese, arguably the greatest rebounder of all time, is on the other side of this matchup.

Per Second Spectrum's rebound tracking, Reese's success rate on offensive rebound attempts has doubled (20% to 40%) when Stokes has gone to the bench in this series — a figure that makes sense considering how small some of the non-Stokes lineups have been for the Valkyries, but it's an eye-popping one nonetheless.

"I think it's always been in her," head coach Natalie Nakase told reporters when asked about Stokes' excellent defensive postseason.

"What she chatted to me before coming [to Golden State] — I know Kiah, obviously, from Vegas — she just needs an environment where she feels good, she feels loved; and I think she feels really connected even though this is her first year with our team."

Nakase went on to laud Stokes for her preparation, experience, and ability to stay centered.

"The biggest thing is, Kiah stays consistent," Nakase said. "She doesn't look for the outside noise; she actually doesn't like attention. With that type of 'star mentality,' I think that's really special and it's what keeps us really focused."

Stokes may not like the attention, but she certainly deserves it.

articles.title: We need more exposure tours: Coach Anitha
articles.body: Bengaluru: Three games, three defeats. For Indian Railways, the FIBA Women’s Basketball League Asia ended without a win, but the tournament offered something the team has never experienced — a closer look at the standards required to compete with Asia’s best.The Indian champions were outplayed by their opponents, with the gulf in physicality, fitness and court craft laid bare. Yet, head coach Anitha Pauldurai believes the experience must be the starting point of a larger push to improve Indian women’s basketball, rather than another disappointing chapter.“The federation has to think beyond preparing just for the Asia Cup. Every year, they have to fix at least five to six exposure tournaments, depending on the calendar. We have to go for more invitation tournaments and exposure trips, especially in the U-16 and U-18 categories,” Anitha said here on Saturday.The Railways team had limited time to train together before the competition. While the initial outing against Japan’s Denso Iris proved a steep learning curve, Anitha felt her players showed better cohesion in subsequent matches.“The way they connected and played in the last two games was important. I am not thinking only about the score, but about how they are playing together. If they get more exposure trips, we can compete better,” she said.The tournament also provided a reality check on conditioning. Anitha pointed out that the Indians began games with energy but struggled to sustain the intensity as the quarters progressed. Playing against stronger opposition, she added, gave the team a benchmark to work towards.Captain Pushpa Senthil Kumar echoed the sentiment, admitting that the lack of experience against top Asian sides had been a major factor. “When we played teams from Japan and Korea, we lost because we did not have any experience playing against them. But we have learnt a lot of things,” Pushpa told TOI.Meanwhile, Rashi Kothari, who scored eight points against Akari Sparks on Saturday, felt the team had improved as the tournament progressed, even if it had not met its own expectations.“As we played more matches, we improved as a team. There are mistakes we need to work on, but with more exposure, we can prove why we are the best team in the country,” she said.The challenge, however, goes beyond a few days of competition. Harshitha Kelttira Bopaiah, who hails from Coorg, pointed to the short preparation camps — often lasting just a month or two — as a major obstacle.She called for a structured grassroots programme and six months to a year of preparation for the national team. “I believe we’re lacking in a grassroots programme. articles.title: Jaylen Brown responds to Jayson Tatum's 'no beef' comments as dispute continues: 'might be a little lamb chops and some gravy'
articles.summary: There still seems to be a little animosity over how Brown's trade from the Celtics.
articles.body:
Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown are in agreement: there's no beef between the former Boston Celtics teammates. But there might be something, judging from Brown's latest comments.

Following the Sixers' 127-116 win over the Milwaukee Bucks , Brown was asked about Tatum's comments the previous night, specifically "This ain't no f***ing Shaq and Kobe. There's no beef."

Brown responded by pointing out that Tatum has a great public relations team, then invoked a different type of meat to describe their relationship :

"We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. There's no beef but it might be a little lamb chops and some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

What does that mean? A reporter asked the natural follow-up question and got this:

"That's what it is. No beef. It should never, ever be that. It's just basketball. We both blessed. But it might be a little lamb chop. We'll be alright."

When asked if he was willing to have a conversation with Tatum, Brown threw out the great PR team line for a second time and the lamb chop line for a third time:

"We both got so much stuff in front of us. At the end of the day, you gotta do what you gotta do for his team. I gotta do what I do for my team. Jayson's a great guy. Like I said, great family. Hell of a basketball player, hell of a PR team. There's no beef. A little lamb chop."

So that's that, we guess, unless Tatum wants to get back into a conversation he very clearly wishes wasn't public, as he said Friday:

"It's turned into this drama type of thing. I got two kids. I reached out to him the day he got traded, I called him, I texted him and I understand people process things differently. At this point in our lives, we're too old to be having our relationship discussed X, Y, Z on the internet. If there's a conversation to be had, we can definitely have that conversation. I welcome that. I've always wanted the best for him and wished the best for him. I've always publicly said those things. I see all these things, 'Get your popcorn ready,' like it's a f***ing boxing match. I play basketball."

"It's turned into this drama type of thing. I got two kids. I reached out to him the day he got traded, I called him, I texted him and I understand people process things differently. At this point in our lives, we're too old to be having our relationship discussed X, Y, Z on the internet. If there's a conversation to be had, we can definitely have that conversation. I welcome that.

I've always wanted the best for him and wished the best for him. I've always publicly said those things. I see all these things, 'Get your popcorn ready,' like it's a f***ing boxing match. I play basketball."

The pair played nine seasons together and won a championship in 2024, but the Brown trade had an air of inevitability. There were always questions about whether the Celtics wanted to carry two wings on supermax contracts in the long term, especially as Brown got older and the team failed to reach the Eastern Conference finals in back-to-back seasons.

Ideally, the franchise would have received something like Giannis Antetokounmpo in return for a former Finals MVP, but that's not how it worked out. All that can be done now is to circle the calendar for these teams' first meeting, as the Celtics are scheduled to host the Sixers on Nov. 10.

articles.title: Caleb Wilson enters in Michael Jordan territory after first 3 NBA games
articles.summary: The Chicago Bulls took on the Washington Wizards in their home opener on Saturday. Although Caleb Wilson soared, finishing with a double-double of 30 points...
articles.body:
The Chicago Bulls took on the Washington Wizards in their home opener on Saturday. Although Caleb Wilson soared, finishing with a double-double of 30 points and 14 rebounds, the Bulls lost 124-120.

However, Wilson showed signs that he indeed can meet or even exceed expectations. Over the course of the first three games, Wilson put up points that put him in the same category as Michael Jordan , no kidding, per Novig. Wilson is now second in points scored through the first three games for a new player with 67. Jordan is first with 74.

Wilson also matched Jordan's numbers in his first two NBA games. Both scored 16 points in their first game and 21 in their second.

At this point, it could be tantalizing to put Wilson in the same category as Jordan, even though he is just getting started and Jordan's legacy needs no explanation. Still, some similarities are worth noting.

For instance, Wilson and Jordan hail out of North Carolina . Both were sensations at Chapel Hill. Jordan was the National Player of the Year in 1984. Meanwhile, Wilson was a second-team All-American in his one year at North Carolina.

Moreover, the Bulls drafted Jordan in 1984 with the No. 3 pick in one of the most consequential drafts in NBA history. Fast forward to 2026, and Wilson was selected No. 4 among one of the best draft classes in recent memory. When Jordan was drafted, he was the solo star for a poor team. Wilson is seen as the savior for a team that has endured years of repeated stagnation.

The Bulls will play the Boston Celtics on Monday, October 26, in Boston.

articles.title: Warriors fall to 0-3 for first time of Stephen Curry's career with loss to Suns
articles.summary: The Warriors' season is not beginning as hoped.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors' season is not beginning as hoped.

The oldest team in the NBA lost 131-122 to the Phoenix Suns on Saturday, pushing their record to 0-3. It's their first streak of three losses to begin a season since 2007-08, meaning this is the first time they have been 0-3 in Stephen Curry's entire career.

Before this season, the Warriors' worst start with Curry was when they went 1-5 to open the 2019-20 season, which is remembered for being the year they were recovering from losing Kevin Durant to free agency and Klay Thompson to an ACL tear before Curry broke his hand in the fourth game. But even in that season, they won their third game.

This season's team came with tempered expectations. Curry and Draymond Green are still around, but Jimmy Butler isn't expected to return from a torn ACL until midseason, while Kristaps Porzingis is still dealing with POTS symptoms . The team's remaining depth is questionable at best.

Saturday's game saw Curry, Green and Brandin Podziemski all sitting out the second leg of a back-to-back. The resulting starting lineup: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Graham Ike, Will Richard and Gui Santos.

That group couldn't stop Suns star Devin Booker from dropping 43 points on 17-of-25 shooting plus 7 rebounds and 7 assists. Golden State had its moments, but a late run in the third quarter put the game out of reach.

The Warriors' entire ethos at this point is maximizing whatever they can get from their once-in-a-generation player in Curry. Last year saw them lose in the play-in tournament with head coach Steve Kerr openly admitting he didn't know what the future held for him, Curry and Green .

Kerr opted to return on a two-year contract rather than retire . He and the rest of the team now have some work to do to avoid a fate even worse than last season, to say nothing of a fifth championship for the team's current era.

articles.title: La primera gran noche de De Larrea en la NBA topa con Wembanyama
articles.standfirst: El base español disputa 33 minutos en ausencia de Flagg e Irving y es el máximo anotador de los Mavericks (21 puntos) en la derrota ante los Spurs
articles.summary: El base español disputa 33 minutos en ausencia de Flagg e Irving y es el máximo anotador de los Mavericks (21 puntos) en la derrota ante los Spurs
articles.body: La primera gran noche de Sergio De Larrea en la NBA no tuvo la recompensa de la victoria. Los Mavericks perdieron por 106-122 frente a los vigentes subcampeones Spurs, que habían comenzado la temporada con dos derrotas. El base español, que venía de haber jugado sólo 56 segundos frente a los Pacers, metió sus primeros puntos en la Liga, pues en los dos primeros partidos no había podido anotar. Saliendo desde el banquillo, 'Larry' fue el máximo anotador de los Mavericks con 21 puntos con 9/15 en tiros de campo. Explotó su recurso de ir hacia canasta y lanzar por elevación desde 4-5 metros. Así evitó alguna vez los larguísimos brazos de Victor Wembanyama. Nadie en los Mavericks hizo más lanzamientos que él. Incluyó un 3/4 en triples. Sumó también cinco rebotes y cuatro asistencias y perdió cuatro balones. Su equipo perdió por cinco puntos en los 33 minutos que permaneció sobre la cancha. Lejos de sentirse satisfecho, el español, protagonista en rueda de prensa, aseguró que tiene que "mejorar muchas cosas. Rotaciones en defensa, estar preparado….Trabajo cada día y hoy creo que fue el resultado de este trabajo”. La presencia de De Larrea en pista durante tantos minutos se explica por las ausencias de las dos estrellas de su equipo, Cooper Flagg y Kyrie Irving. El primero, mejor rookie de la temporada pasada, se lesionó un hombro tras recibir una dura personal en el último encuentro cuando se disponía a hacer un mate. Se perderá al menos una semana. Y el segundo, tuvo descanso en el segundo en noches consecutivas. Viene de una lesión de rodilla que le ha tenido 19 meses de baja. La mala noche de los titulares, con 50 puntos entre todos, hizo que el entrenador Dusty May mirara más al banquillo. El técnico acabó muy satisfecho con la actuación del español: "Pienso que fue genial. Su defensa está mejorando, sobre todo sobre el portador del balón. Estaba persiguiendo rebotes largos En general, fue un partido realmente bueno de un jugador joven contra una de las mejores defensas en la línea de fondo". Los suplentes plantaron cara a los Spurs hasta el último cuarto. Wembanyama, con 23 puntos, siete rebotes y cuatro tapones, fue el mejor en las filas de San Antonio. Dylan Harper anotó 22 puntos y De'Aaron Fox y Stephon Castle llegaron a los 19. Pese a sus actuaciones, el partido no se decidió hasta el periodo final. Los Spurs dominaron casi siempre y llegaron a tener una ventaja de 23 puntos. En el tercer acto desperdiciaron una renta de 14. Daniel Gafford llegó a colocar a uno a los Mavericks con la primera canasta del último cuarto (91-92), pero después los visitantes metieron cinco de sus 15 triples de la noche. Dallas no pudo mantener el ritmo anotador de Harper y Julian Champagnie. Cuando De Larrea saltó a la pista en el periodo definitivo ya estaba todo cuesta arriba (94-103) y el parcial inicial fue creciendo del 0-11 al 6-18 para fijar un 98-119 ya inalcanzable para los locales.

articles.title: Antetokounmpo tampoco se estrena a la tercera con los Heat, colistas del Este
articles.standfirst: El griego todavía no sabe lo que es ganar con su nuevo equipo después de tres partidos
articles.summary: El griego todavía no sabe lo que es ganar con su nuevo equipo después de tres partidos
articles.body: El movimiento de Giannis Antetokounmpo firmando por los Heat fue uno de los más trascendentes del convulso mercado del pasado verano. El coloso griego dejaba atrás toda una vida en Milwaukee para irse a Miami. Su fichaje multiplicaba las opciones de su equipo de luchar por el anillo. Sin embargo, el inicio de curso está siendo terrible: tres partidos y todavía no sabe lo que es ganar. Tras perder por 25 en el arranque de la temporada en casa ante los Timberwolves y por 17 frente a los Pistons en el segundo partido como locales, los Heat cayeron también en su primera salida. Derrota por 115-110 contra los Hornets, con importantes bajas y que la noche anterior habían perdido por 47 ante los Hawks. Ese 0-3 deja a Miami como colista de la Conferencia Este. Pronto, sí, pero conviene que arranque cuanto antes. Antetokounmpo se quedó sólo en 14 puntos con 4/11 en tiros. Disputó sólo 25 minutos por problemas de faltas y mientras estuvo en pista los Heat tuvieron un balance de -20. Davion Mitchell, con 22 puntos y 10 asistencias, y Bam Adebayo, con 20 puntos y ocho rebotes, fueron los puntales de Miami Brandon Miller, que venía de fallar 12 de sus 14 tiros de campo incluidos 10 de sus 11 triples en el partido anterior, recuperó la puntería y acabó con 34 puntos para liderar el triunfo de Charlotte. Junto a él brillaron el alemán Dennis Schroder (25), Naz Reid (23) y Grayson Allen (20). Entre todos ellos le dieron una máxima a su equipo de 23 puntos cuando finalizaba el tercer cuarto (96-73). La remontada de los Heat en el último periodo llegó con Antetokounmpo en el banquillo debido a la acumulación de personales. Los visitantes llegaron a empatar a 100. Después, con cinco minutos por jugarse y el marcador aún parejo, regresó el griego a la pista, aunque fue eliminado poco después. Antes de irse fue testigo cercano de un acrobático 3+1 de Grayson Allen que fue un puñal para los Heat.

articles.title: Los Sixers también ganan sin LeBron
articles.standfirst: Embiid (28 puntos), Brown (27) y Maxey (26) acaban con los Bucks en la primera noche sin el mito
articles.summary: Embiid (28 puntos), Brown (27) y Maxey (26) acaban con los Bucks en la primera noche sin el mito
articles.body: Los Sixers sumaron su tercera victoria consecutiva para abrir la temporada tras deshacerse de los Bucks (127-116). Los de Filadelfia no echaron demasiado de menos a LeBron James, que se perdió su primer partido del curso debido a la ciática arrastra desde hace tiempo. El mito, que está a poco más de un mes de cumplir los 42 años, se perdió los primeros 14 encuentros de la temporada pasada debido a esa dolencia. Así que los Sixers decidieron darle descanso en la primera noche de partidos consecutivos. Mejor que se tomara libre un duelo ante los Bucks que uno frente a los Pistons. Sin él, los otros tres pilares del equipo de Filadelfia se la apañaron para resolver: 81 puntos entre Joel Embiid, que hizo un triple con 28+11+10, Jaylen Brown, que llegó a los 27, y Tyrese Maxey, que metió 26. VJ Edgecombe se quedó en 17. Completó el quinteto inicial, en lugar de LeBron, Dean Wade, que no había jugado en los dos primeros partidos por lesión. Los Sixers tuvieron que esperar a los últimos minutos para atar el triunfo. Brown puso el 120-114 con un triple tras a pase de Embiid que certificaba su triple-doble. Después, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope anotó nuevamente desde el perímetro y colocó la diferencia en unos nueve puntos que ya fueron insalvables para los Bucks. Milwaukee, único equipo del Este junto a los Heat que aún no ha ganado después de tres encuentros, tuvo a Jaime Jáquez Jr., con 21 puntos, como jugador más destacado. Los dobles-dobles de Kel'el Ware (19+13) y Kyle Kuzma (14+12) tampoco bastaron.

articles.title: Jokic roza los 200 triples-dobles y carga contra sus aficionados: "Ya no son bienvenidos"
articles.standfirst: Jamal Murray (42 puntos) y el pívot (35+15+10) lideran el triunfo en la prórroga de los Nuggets, que llegaron a perder por 23 entre abucheos de su público
articles.summary: Jamal Murray (42 puntos) y el pívot (35+15+10) lideran el triunfo en la prórroga de los Nuggets, que llegaron a perder por 23 entre abucheos de su público
articles.body: El estreno en casa de los Nuggets fue de lo más convulso. Los locales llegaron a estar 23 puntos abajo frente a los Pelicans (30-53) entre abucheos de sus propios aficionados. Después llegaría una gran remontada en la segunda parte, un triunfo en la prórroga y las críticas de Nikola Jokic a quienes silbaron al equipo. "Nos abuchearon en nuestro primer partido en casa, y creo que esos aficionados ya no tienen por qué venir. Si nos siguen, saben que nunca nos rendimos y que nos hemos recuperado de situaciones mucho peores. Así que, si me preguntan, ya no son bienvenidos", dijo el pívot serbio, que acabó con 35 puntos, ocho de ellos en la prórroga, 15 rebotes y 10 asistencias. Fue su triple-doble número 199 en su carrera NBA, lo que le coloca ya a sólo 10 del récord de Russell Westbrook. Si no hay contratiempos, lo batirá esta temporada. El otro artífice de la gesta fue Jamal Murray, que anotó 42 puntos. Y papel importante también el del novato Trevon Brazile, que hizo siete de sus 17 puntos en el tiempo extra, incluido un triple clave para que los Nuggets se colocaran con cuatro puntos arriba (133-129) a falta de 1:25 para el final. Jokic no encontraba explicación a la mala primera parte de su equipo. "Simplemente, nada te sale bien. Ellos encestan y tú no. Había mala energía y necesitas que pasen un par de minutos para poder salir de ahí", analizó el pívot. Los Pelicans tuvieron un 65,9% de aciertos en tiros de campo en la primera mitad, lo que habla bastante mal de la defensa local. Al descanso ganaban por 57-73. A la salida de los vestuarios, Jokic y Murray se pusieron al mando de la operaciones. Metieron 22 de los 32 puntos de Denver en el tercer periodo, pero ni así consiguieron recortar demasiado. Los de Nueva Orleans, liderados por Trey Murphy (26) y Dejounte Murray (22) aún estaban 19 arriba poco después del arranque del último periodo (91-110). Un triple de Murray y un mate de Aaron Gordon pusieron a los Nuggets a la estela de su rival. El escolta, con dos tiros libres a falta de 16 segundos, fijó el empate a 126 y Murphy perdió el balón en el último ataque de los Pelicans. En la prórroga, entre Jokic y Brazile metieron los 15 puntos de Denver y los espectadores del Ball Arena convirtieron los abucheos en ovaciones. Al serbio, los primeros no se le olvidan.

images.caption: Jamal Murray busca un pase ante la defensa de DeAndre Jordan. LAPRESSE

articles.title: Los Warriors consuman su peor inicio en la era Curry
articles.standfirst: Plagados de bajas, incluida la de su estrella, suman su tercera derrota seguida para abrir la temporada
articles.summary: Plagados de bajas, incluida la de su estrella, suman su tercera derrota seguida para abrir la temporada
articles.body: Por primera vez desde la temporada 2007-08, los Warriors han comenzado una temporada perdiendo sus tres primeros encuentros. Se trata del peor inicio de la franquicia en la era Stephen Curry, que llegó al equipo en 2009. Si nada cambia, la estrella de 38 años, que no jugó en la derrota ante los Suns por 131-122, podría vivir uno de los cursos más frustrantes de su carrera, con el equipo muy lejos de poder aspirar a algo. En el tercer partido en cuatro noches, los Warriors decidieron dar descanso a muchos de sus jugadores importantes. Curry no jugó al estar tocado de la rodilla derecha mientras que Brandin Podziemski y otros dos veteranos como Draymond Green y Al Horford sufrían problemas de espalda. A ellos hay que sumar a Jimmy Butler, al que no se espera hasta bien entrada la temporada tras romperse en enero el ligamento cruzado anterior de la rodilla derecha, y a Kristaps Porzingis, que hasta se está planteando la retirada al no remitir los síntomas de un desorden del sistema nervioso que le provoca cansancio, taquicardias y mareos. Con semejante parte médico, la única buena noticia en este inicio de campaña para los Warriors es la irrupción del novato Yaxel Landeborg. Si en el primer partido se atravió a retar a Luka Doncic, en los dos siguientes ha dado muestras de sus capacidades: 18+13+6 ante los Grizzlies y 26+9+5 en la derrota frente a los Suns. De'Anthony Melton, con 25 puntos, también destacó. El partido lo desequilibró Devin Booker, autor de 43 puntos (17 de 25 tiros de campo), 17 de ellos en el tercer cuarto, que acabó con 102-92. Los Warriors aguantaron hasta que Luke Kennard anotó uno de sus tres triples para distanciar a los Suns 15 puntos arriba a falta de seis minutos. Los Warriors ya no tuvieron capacidad de reacción y sellaron su peor comienzo de temporada en 19 años, aunque el entrenador Steve Kerr no se rinde: "Es sólo proceso. Sigamos poniendo el trabajo. Aprenderemos de esto, pero no vamos a perder nuestro espíritu".

images.caption: Devin Booker lanza ante la defensa de Georges Niang. LAPRESSE

articles.title: Otro récord espera a Llull
articles.standfirst: El capitán del Real Madrid está a punto de rebasar a Juan Carlos Navarro como el jugador con más partidos en ACB con un mismo club
articles.summary: El capitán del Real Madrid está a punto de rebasar a Juan Carlos Navarro como el jugador con más partidos en ACB con un mismo club
articles.body: Otro récord espera a Sergio Llull si juega este domingo (19.00 horas) en el Barris Nord en la visita del Real Madrid al iLerna Lleida. Con saltar a la cancha, se convertirá en el jugador que más partidos haya disputado con un mismo equipo en la historia de la ACB. Actualmente se encuentra igualado con Juan Carlos Navarro, que vivió 689 con el Barcelona. El base menorquín lleva esa misma cifra con la camiseta madridista y añade a su total otros 11 con el Manresa, los primeros de su carrera. El capitán blanco, que sale casi a récord por partido, llegó a los 700 encuentros en la ACB la semana pasada frente al Surne Bilbao Basket. Es el sexto jugador que llega a esa cifra. Por delante, su excompañero Felipe Reyes, Rafa Jofresa, Nacho Rodríguez, Marcelinho Huertas y Nacho Azofra. Todos ellos pasaron por varios equipos o no tuvieron etapas tan longevas como la de Llull en el Madrid. Son ya 21 temporadas en el club. Camino de los 39 años, que cumplirá a mediados de noviembre, el base todavía no se ha estrenado esta campaña en la Euroliga, pero sí es un fijo en la Liga Endesa, donde ha participado en los cuatro encuentros disputados hasta ahora para firmar nuevos récords o engordar los que ya posee. Aunque su físico ya no es el que era, Llull sigue confirmando que puede ofrecer momentos contados de calidad. En la última jornada fue el mejor del Madrid en la aplastante victoria contra el Surne Bilbao terminando con 19 puntos y 5/9 en triples en sólo 12:37 minutos en pista. Más allá de sus estadísticas, es su ascendencia y su ejemplo para el vestuario lo más valioso para el equipo. Los galones son suyos. El Madrid, mientras, intentará mantener la buena dinámica en la que ha entrado. No pierde desde la visita al Hapoel Tel Aviv el 31 de septiembre y suma ocho victorias consecutivas. En la Liga Endesa se mantiene como único invicto después de las cuatro primeras jornadas y ha firmado un arranque histórico en lo ofensivo promediando 110,5 puntos de media. Frenar a esa locomotora es el difícil reto del iLerna Lleida.

articles.title: 1 Prediction Every NBA Fanbase Is Going To Hate
articles.summary: Just as we know the 2026-27 NBA season will feature first-time All-Stars, broken records and award-worthy play, we can be sure it'll also include its share of disappointments.
articles.body:
Just as we know the 2026-27 NBA season will feature first-time All-Stars, broken records and award-worthy play, we can be sure it'll also include its share of disappointments.

After spending an offseason forecasting the positive, we need to jump in during the early part of the year to balance the scales. That's right: It's time to predict some negative outcomes.

Here, we'll take a shot at something that'll work out worse than expected for every team. Maybe it's a guess about the downside of a risky transaction by, say, the Los Angeles Lakers. Or maybe we'll pour cold water on what may come after the Boston Celtics' likely regular-season success.

Let's check in on what will go wrong for each team as the 2026-27 season unfolds.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LA Clippers | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

Atlanta Hawks: No Late-Season Snacks Available

The Atlanta Hawks fattened up on junk food late last year, going 18-2 from Feb. 22 to April 3. Among their victims during that surge were Brooklyn, Milwaukee, Memphis, Sacramento, Washington and Dallas—all teams that had completely abandoned the goal of winning games.

That run was key to getting the Hawks up to 46 wins and the No. 6 seed in the East. Without it, they could very easily have finished behind the 43-win Miami Heat and missed the postseason entirely.

Thanks to lottery reform, teams like the ones Atlanta hammered down the stretch will no longer be trying to lose on purpose. That doesn't necessarily mean the Hawks are destined to disappoint, but it does suggest they'll have to earn their way back to the playoffs.

This time around, nobody's going to hand them a bunch of empty-calorie wins.

Boston Celtics: They'll Miss Jaylen Brown...Eventually

It wouldn't be a surprise if the Boston Celtics won more regular season games this year than last. Their emphasis on winning the possession battle and dominating the shot-math game will only intensify without Jaylen Brown, who tended to pepper in more isolation actions than head coach Joe Mazzulla seemed to prefer.

We should expect Jayson Tatum to fit more snugly into Boston's three-hunting offense than Brown did, and growth from several young players—Baylor Scheierman, Ron Harper Jr., Hugo Gonzalez, Jordan Walsh—could make for a bottomlessly deep rotation.

If Mitchell Robinson's offensive rebounding creates even more kick-out three-point opportunities, long-range shooting records could fall.

All of that will be fine and dandy during the year, but Boston will run into trouble during the postseason when defenses are better at forcing opponents out of their preferred styles. Maybe it won't matter until the second round, but the Celtics will miss Brown's individual shot creation and on-ball defense at some point.

Keep that in mind as Boston racks up wins from October to April and Brown's absence occasionally feels like addition by subtraction.

Brooklyn Nets: Lottery Reform Will Wreck the Season

Broadly, the lottery tweaks that disincentivize the most egregious and prolonged brand of tanking are a good thing. For the Brooklyn Nets, specifically, they shouldn't change what's been a years-long attempt to lose games.

Brooklyn owes its 2027 first-round pick to the Houston Rockets. Under the old system, Brooklyn would have felt a sense of freedom (it could lose or win as much as it wanted, since the pick would be gone either way), but the new one makes finishing in the bottom three the best course of action.

If Brooklyn isn't in the relegation zone, its odds of winning (and conveying) the No. 1 overall pick are greater than if it lands in the bottom three. If the Nets win the lottery, they wouldn't be allowed to in 2028—when they actually control their pick.

That means another year of tanking is on the horizon.

Heat, Giannis were down by 20+ in each of their 3 losses

Charlotte Hornets: The Offense Is In Trouble

Maybe things will balance out over the course of the season as the Charlotte Hornets' revamped core gets fully healthy. At the outset, though, it will be tough to recreate the high-scoring style that defined the team last season.

LaMelo Ball is gone via trade. While the move might ultimately position the Hornets to reach a higher level than they could have with the dynamic point guard, it will probably diminish their scoring punch in the short term.

Kon Knueppel's preseason hamstring strain and Coby White's calf tweak will all but assure offensive slippage.

Last year, Charlotte's elite attack fell to below-average scoring rates when Ball and Knueppel were both off the floor. That'll be the default more often at the start of the year. Things may not get back on track for a while as the Hornets adjust to their new circumstances.

Chicago Bulls: Shooting Will Be a Problem Again

The Chicago Bulls hit 35.6 percent of their threes last year, a bottom-10 figure that was only partially offset by a shot diet focused on lots of threes and layups. Even after adding Norman Powell in free agency, the Bulls seem primed for similar struggles on the perimeter.

Josh Giddey doesn't worry defenses, even as his percentage ticks up. Caleb Wilson's apparent ability to hit from outside is welcome, but opponents will dare him to fire until he proves he's a true threat. Matas Buzelis is only theoretically dangerous. Nic Claxton has never been a gunner.

If the Bulls can't generate good spacing, their half-court attack will suffer. Lanes will close for Buzelis and Wilson. Claxton's elbow game won't work as well on a cramped floor, as clean looks will generally be tough to come by.

Cleveland Cavaliers: James Harden Will James Harden

James Harden is a person, which makes him a noun. James Harden can also be a verb, as in: "That player failed to show up for a critical playoff game. He really James Hardened on that one."

Or, alternatively: "Is this guy going to James Harden us by demanding a trade midway through his contract?"

The Cleveland Cavaliers committed three years and $90 million to the noun version of Harden over the summer, which means they also signed up for three years of wondering when (not if) James Harden will James Harden them.

If you're looking for a fatal flaw in Cleveland's would-be contending roster, it's right there. At some point this year, one way or the other, James Harden is going to James Harden. It's inevitable.

Dallas Mavericks: Cooper Flagg's Life Won't Get Easier

Overburdened as a playmaker from the jump last year, Cooper Flagg still produced one of the greatest seasons by a teenager in NBA history. Though Kyrie Irving is back and new head coach Dusty May should have some fresh ideas, Flagg's second season will likely be as taxing as his first.

Irving's presence isn't the major load-lightener it seems. He's 34 and coming off a serious injury. Though preseason play suggested Irving still has plenty of juice, the Mavs will be careful not to overplay the veteran guard. Then there's the possibility of a mid-season trade removing Irving from the equation and thrusting Flagg right back into the do-everything role he occupied last year.

A roster overloaded with forwards, lacking guard play and quietly facing depth issues at center, as long as Dereck Lively II's health remains a question mark, will again force Flagg into difficult spots. In the unlikely event more shot-creators and finishers emerge, it'll just mean Flagg can use his energy to defend tougher assignments on the other end.

Denver Nuggets: Contention Isn't Realistic

We've moved past the point where having Nikola Jokić on the roster automatically makes the Denver Nuggets title contenders.

That's not so much a statement about Jokić's ability as he enters his age-31 season. He's still a short-list MVP candidate who's all but guaranteed to keep the Nuggets' offense inside the top three. Instead, it's an acknowledgment that years of unwise spending and salary-cutting trades have led to a critical lack of depth, defense and athleticism.

Denver ranked 21st in defensive efficiency last year. Swapping Peyton Watson for DeMar DeRozan won't improve that ranking. Aaron Gordon and Christian Braun could stay healthier, but Jokić showed real slippage on D in 2025-26. You could make the case that, all things being equal, the Nuggets could manage something like the 17th or 18th-best defense with a few breaks.

That, even if paired with a No. 1 offense, won't be enough.

Detroit Pistons: Shooting Won't Cure Everything

The Detroit Pistons' offseason suggested they thought suspect shooting was their only problem last year. That feels like a mistake.

Lots of numbers show the Pistons needed better spacing. For example, the offense was 10.2 points per 100 possessions better last year whenever sharpshooter Duncan Robinson was in the game. That's why going out and getting Isaiah Joe, John Collins, Gary Harris and Taurean Prince—all 40.0 percent snipers—made sense.

All that shooting will only matter if someone not named Cade Cunningham can break down the defense off the dribble and set up a teammate.

Based on the risky five-year, $155 million extension they gave Ausar Thompson, the Pistons believe he can handle increased distribution duties. He's a speculative facilitator, at best. Daniss Jenkins broke out last year, but he's still the team's only proven creator besides Cunningham.

Detroit's offense has more weapons, but it didn't add the kinds of players who can utilize them. That's not going to be a problem during the regular season, but the Pistons are going to struggle to score in the playoffs.

Golden State Warriors: Steph, Jimmy and Porzingis Won't Play Together

If Jimmy Butler is back on the floor just before the trade deadline, that'll leave about 30 games left before the end of the regular season. If Stephen Curry and Kristaps Porzingis are relatively healthy at that point, they could be expected to play in 20-25 of those contests.

Maybe the stars will align, with rest nights not overlapping too often and the trio could share the floor 15 times or so. That's the optimistic outlook.

More realistically, Butler could be traded before or shortly after he returns (assuming that's before the deadline). If that happens, this prediction will be automatically correct. We also have to consider the possibility that a recurrence of runner's knee limits Curry as often as last year, when he logged just 43 games.

Porzingis remains out indefinitely to start the season.

These three, arguably Golden State's best players when available, aren't going to share the floor at all.

Houston Rockets: Amen Thompson Won't Improve

If the Houston Rockets factored improvement into their calculations on Amen Thompson's $208 million extension, they're going to regret it.

Sure, the 23-year-old is at an age where growth is typically priced in. But Thompson is a player who thrives mainly on the strength of his athleticism, and that's not a characteristic that trends up over time. As a shooter, Thompson appears to be a lost cause. He attempted just 1.4 threes per 36 minutes last season, down from his first two years, and converted them at a 21.6 percent clip.

So if Thompson isn't going to get more athletic, and if he's never going to be a perimeter threat, it's hard to imagine how he might improve his performance. Considering he led the league in total minutes last year, he won't grow by adding volume.

The good news: Thompson is an elite perimeter defender who can pass the ball and impact the game in transition. He'll be a starting-caliber performer for the life of his deal. Anyone anticipating some kind of leap that might justify his price tag will be disappointed.

Indiana Pacers: Kelly Oubre Jr. Won't Fit

The Indiana Pacers badly needed a bigger wing to compete against Eastern Conference foes with rangier, more physically imposing forwards. In that sense, Kelly Oubre Jr. fills an important role.

In several others, he's going to feel like a square peg in a round hole.

Basketball She Wrote's Caitlin Cooper highlighted the way Oubre's strong preference for driving from the right wing clashes with some of Indiana's most effective actions. This deep into his career, Oubre may struggle to adjust. More broadly, the lefty wing has never been a quick processor or intuitive passer on offense.

Oubre averaged 3.44 seconds per touch and about one pass for every minute he played last season, figures that don't jive with Indy's tendency to keep the ball moving at high speed.

Don't be surprised if Oubre, despite prized size and athleticism, doesn't find himself on the floor in key moments.

Other than Darius Garland looking like the best version of himself during the preseason, the LA Clippers didn't see many early positive signs.

Brandon Ingram, Max Strus, Jordan Miller and Yanic Konan NIederhauser are all out for extended periods, Bradley Beal is dealing with knee inflammation and the center rotation of Isaiah Jackson and Brook Lopez might be among the weakest in the league.

The Clips are out five future first-rounders and probably wouldn't want to deal any picks to improve in the short term anyway. They're in for a protracted rebuild in which perhaps only rookie Keaton Wagler features as a long-term building block.

There are plenty of teams in for rough seasons, some of which are with the Clips out West. But as it stands now, it's difficult to imagine LA cobbling together more than 30 wins if almost everything broke right from here.

Los Angeles Lakers: Walker Kessler Isn't Worth It

Wait, so Walker Kessler won't be worth $130 million over four years, or won't be worth the two unprotected firsts and two swaps the Los Angeles Lakers surrendered for the right to pay him all that money?

Pick one. It doesn't really matter for our purposes. The point here is that the Lakers gave up entirely too much, burning cap space and firing off their last tradable picks for a player who, while very good at his role, is not a needle-moving star.

The desperation that motivated such a reckless move is understandable. The Lakers lost LeBron James and needed to appease Luka Dončić by landing a big man who could anchor the defense and finish inside. Kessler does both well.

Unfortunately, Kessler's niche skills won't be nearly enough to make Los Angeles relevant in the championship picture. And that's where a team that just made a trade as consequential as the one that landed him should wind up.

For the deal to be worth it, Kessler would need to stay healthy all year, feature prominently on the DPOY short list and carry the Lakers to a top-five defensive rating. There's no way that's happening.

Memphis Grizzlies: Playmaking Is a Key Weakness

Playmaking is one of rookie Cam Boozer's biggest strengths, but the first-year forward will find himself having to do way too much creation in a Memphis offense that could quickly find itself hurting in that area.

Ty Jerome's herky-jerky floater arsenal will work just fine as long as he's healthy. He racked up 45 points in Memphis' opener as proof.

This feels like a good time to mention he's played fewer than 50 games in all but one of his seven professional seasons. And while Scotty Pippen Jr. is a luxury backup, most of his contributions come on the defensive end.

Boozer can and should be used as a hub on offense, but the Grizzlies also need to surround him with guards who can initiate actions. Between Jerome and Pippen, it's hard to be confident in Boozer's support system.

The Miami Heat may not mind if a leap from Pelle Larsson is the reason free-agent signee Klay Thompson isn't in the game during the biggest moments. But it'll be a problem if Thompson's continued decline is the main explanation.

Thompson is unquestionably one of the greatest shooters in history, but last year saw him post career lows in field-goal and three-point percentage. Diminished lateral mobility meant Thompson could only guard power forwards, and the days of him scaring defenses as a cutter and inside-the-arc scorer appear long gone.

Tim Hardaway Jr. seems like the better option at this point if the Heat feel they need a shooter on the floor in the late going. Larsson is younger and more complete as an on-ball option, but he has yet to build a reputation as a spot-up threat.

Thompson could surprise with a bounce-back year, but most of the evidence suggests he's not going to be Miami's best option as a fifth closer alongside Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins.

The Milwaukee Bucks did well to haul in so many assets in the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade, but the next phase of their rebuild won't be as simple as it seems.

Normally, the Bucks would focus on juicing the value of the players they acquired in order to trade them for picks and more future-focused assets. Because so many of them overlap positionally, the process of upping one player's market appeal could come at the cost of others. In other words, it won't be easy to maximize Tyler Herro's minutes and production without taking away from Kasparas Jakucionis'—particularly with Ryan Rollins also deserving a major role at a guard spot.

The Bucks also need to give rookie Brayden Burries a ton of minutes after selecting him 10th in the draft.

On a squad that'll be losing lots of games while trying to apportion playing time, it won't be easy to build up the trade values of the players Milwaukee needs to move.

Minnesota Timberwolves: Jonathan Kuminga Will Lose His Starting Job

The Minnesota Timberwolves will soon become the third team to learn that Jonathan Kuminga is not a reliable starter.

It took the Golden State Warriors four-and-a-half years to embrace that truth, but the Atlanta Hawks figured it out in a matter of weeks. Minnesota might accept reality even more quickly.

Kuminga has immense physical tools. He's a huge wing with boundless athleticism and the ability to power his way to the free-throw line. He also wants to play like a first option—one who generates his own shots off the dribble. The Warriors wanted him to leverage his athletic gifts in a do-it-all support role, which clashed with Kuminga's own opinions on how he should be used.

Minnesota didn't invest a lottery pick or any significant money in Kuminga, so it's not as committed as the Warriors once were. At the same time, the Wolves' very real depth issues at forward make Kuminga pretty important to the whole operation.

He'll begin the season as a starter, but that won't last long.

New Orleans Pelicans: Zion Williamson's Dunk Rate Will Fall

A small year-over-year uptick saw Zion Williamson dunk 10.3 percent of his field-goal attempts last season, better than the 8.5 percent he managed in 2024-25. Do not take that increase as evidence Williamson is on the way to reclaiming peak athletic form.

The days of Williamson posting dunk rates in the teens are in the past, and the longer arc of his athletic prowess continues to bend downward. Anecdotally, the relatively healthy version of Zion who played 62 games last year didn't have the same shocking burst or force that he showed at his apex.

That's not a surprise, given the conditioning issues and (probably) related injuries that marked most of his early 20s. Now 26, the likelihood of a trend reversal in the speed and lift departments is basically nil.

Pair that "Father Time is undefeated" fact with Williamson's total abandonment of his jump shot, and defenders will sag off to a degree that makes running over and through them even harder than it once was.

Even before the New York Knicks disappointed Karl-Anthony Towns by surprising him with a public announcement that extension negotiations were officially tabled, the odds of a repeat championship were slim.

Now, with the vibes feeling less than immaculate, New York seems assured of being the eighth straight champion to relinquish the title.

The Knicks are coming off a 100-game season in which they authored multiple high-stress postseason comebacks. They lost key contributor Mitchell Robinson over money and feature several core players on the wrong side of 30.

Jalen Brunson is one of those, and while it's impossible to count him out, the sheer toll of playing such a high-usage style while battling through what feel like 15 ankle sprains per season is bound to catch up with him eventually. And as is so often the case, several other Knicks played at a level that could be fairly described as "over their heads" en route to the 2026 championship.

You can't assume everyone will be able to find that same rare form again, particularly given the fatigue of a deep run and exhausting offseason media tour.

Oklahoma City Thunder: Cason Wallace Doesn't Have Hidden Skills

Cason Wallace has never averaged more than the 8.6 points and 2.6 assists per game he posted last season, and it's a mistake to assume he's primed for a statistical spike in what should be a larger role this year.

The idea that Wallace has had to settle for a smaller, more dependent role than his skills warrant isn't completely off base. Playing with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Chet Holmgren and Jalen Williams means virtually everyone else has to slot into a lower-usage position.

But very little about Wallace's profile suggests he's got some dormant set of skills just waiting to be unleashed.

Last year, lineups featuring Wallace without SGA and J-Dub scored 11.6 points per 100 possessions, a 24th percentile figure. In games where Wallace, who averaged 26.6 minutes per game, played between 30 and 39 minutes , he only managed 12.5 points and 3.7 assists.

Wallace is a tremendous defensive guard who can reliably hit spot-up threes. He's not going to turn into some kind of top-tier offensive threat now that minutes vacated by Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe are available.

Orlando Magic: Cap Casualties Are Coming

Anthony Black is a player the Orlando Magic should want to keep around, but their bloated books made a preseason extension too costly to consider. If the rangy guard sticks with the team, it'll be after a restricted free-agency scenario next summer.

If Black plays so well this season as to make himself indispensable, there's a great chance another of Orlando's key figures has to go. The Magic could have as much as $193 million committed to just eight players ahead of 2027-28, in which case a $20 million salary for Black would exceed the luxury tax line. And that's without filling out the rest of the roster.

If the Magic dramatically disappoint, anyone from Paolo Banchero to Franz Wagner to Jalen Suggs could be on the move.

The Thunder had already accomplished far more than this Magic team when they initiated some cost-cutting triage. Expect Orlando to trim real talent one way or the other.

Philadelphia 76ers: Joel Embiid Won't Help

For years, the key factor in analyzing the Philadelphia 76ers' potential for the upcoming season was the number of games Joel Embiid would be able to play. Based on what we've seen from the former MVP over the last couple of years, quantity is no longer the lone issue.

The quality of Embiid's performance isn't going to be good enough for him to matter all that much.

In his first preseason game against the Brooklyn Nets on Oct. 8, Embiid missed four of his five attempts from the field, coughed the ball up eight times in 23 minutes and could hardly get off the ground. He hasn't been nearly that bad since, but it was no less jarring to watch considering Embiid was theoretically fresh after a full, injury-free offseason.

Embiid should still be able to make spot-up shots and hit some elbow jumpers out of a triple-threat position, and he probably won't average a turnover every three minutes once he's accustomed to his new teammates. His defense was encouraging in the Sixers' opener against the Knicks.

But all the injuries he's suffered over the years have degraded his game to the point that availability is now only one of the worries Philly has to consider.

Phoenix Suns: Worse Record than Last Year

The Phoenix Suns are among the teams most likely to be hurt by tanking reform, as the 24-7 record they ran up against losing teams last year won't be easy to replicate.

In addition to facing fewer record-boosting pushovers this time around, the Suns could also struggle to catch teams of all abilities off guard. It's certainly not a bad thing to be known for playing hard, but Phoenix snuck up on plenty of opponents with its aggression last year. Nobody will be taken unawares this time around.

Toss in some other factors—more Jalen Green may not be a good thing, youngster Khaman Maluach may not be ready for the big role coming his way, Dillon Brooks is freshly paid, etc.—and there are a whole bunch of reasons to expect a worse record than last year's 45-37 mark.

Portland Trail Blazers: Deni Avdija's Role Will Shrink

Deni Avdija led the NBA with 27.8 drives per game last season, and his hard-charging, ball-dominant style was key to the Portland Trail Blazers' limited offensive success.

Instead of surrounding Avdija with a gaggle of shooters following his All-Star leap, the Blazers will instead integrate two high-usage guards who've only ever been effective with the ball in their hands.

Forget the obviously terrible fit of Damian Lillard and Ja Morant on the court together. The real issue here is the way neither of those players complement Portland's clear No. 1 option. At least in theory, Lillard has the shooting skill to provide off-ball value. But he's never played that role for any sustained length of time.

Morant isn't helpful unless he's controlling the offense.

Injuries could paradoxically solve the problem, but nobody should be rooting for Dame and Morant to miss time. As it stands, the Blazers' best player is in for a reduced role. Make it make sense.

Sacramento Kings: There's No Trading Out of This Mess

The Sacramento Kings often feel like the biggest victims of lottery reform. They're going to be terrible as usual, only now they're less likely to be rewarded with a high draft pick. The counter would be: They failed to figure out how to win in 20-plus years of the old system, so nobody should feel bad for them in the new one.

If you're still inclined to be sympathetic, there's another angle: Sacramento also can't trade its way out of this mess.

The Kings already bought out DeMar DeRozan, and they may need to do the same with Zach LaVine and his much larger salary. Nobody is sending positive value to Sacramento for $49 million worth of empty scoring.

Domantas Sabonis has two years and $94 million left on his deal, and he's also a negative asset.

Unless somebody wants De'Andre Hunter's expiring money or believes Malik Monk could get back to his best days as a star Sixth Man, the Kings don't have anything worth dealing.

San Antonio Spurs: The Three-Guard Lineup Will Pose Problems

Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell and Victor Wembanyama are probably the San Antonio Spurs' five best players, but they do not make up the team's best lineup. Despite that, head coach Mitch Johnson seems committed to starting them together.

Fox's postseason struggles and Harper's simultaneous emergence as a potential superstar created a tricky dynamic. The former is too established and highly paid to come off the bench, while the latter is simply too good. Even if it doesn't necessarily lead the team in minutes, this lineup might be necessary just to avoid bruising egos.

Tactically, it's exciting to get three playmaking guards on the floor together. But all three of Fox, Harper and Castle come with questions about their three-point shots, and using all of them at once means there's no longer a setup man coming off the bench.

Another concern: San Antonio keeps exploring the idea of using Wembanyama as an initiator, which doesn't play to his strengths as an elite play-finisher. He started 0-of-12 in San Antonio's opener against the Thunder.

Plopping three suspect-shooting guards on the perimeter certainly doesn't make things easier for Wemby.

The assembled talent is so good that the whole thing might work anyway. But it's a mistake to think this is the smoothest, most sensible way for the Spurs to play.

Toronto Raptors: Kawhi Won't Be There When It Counts

The Toronto Raptors are going to have a hellaciously good defense, and a load-managed Kawhi Leonard will provide the offense with an organizing central figure whenever he's available. Those two factors should lead to a whole mess of regular season wins.

The issue for the Raptors, who'll be able to play with virtually anyone from October to April, is that Leonard won't be able to help them outside that six-month window.

That's what recent history suggests, anyway.

Leonard finished the 2025 postseason healthy, a notable feat because it was the only time since the 2020 bubble that he held up through the end of the year. For the vast majority of his seasons with LA, Leonard broke down before the conclusion of the campaign.

So while Toronto has the makings of an every-night behemoth, it can't be counted on to profile as a contender. Leonard simply hasn't been a reliable postseason presence. Unless he bucks that trend, the Raptors aren't a true title threat.

Utah Jazz: This Is A Bottom-Five Defense

The Utah Jazz will be trying to win games this season, but effort isn't everything.

A pair of guards who certainly aren't notable for their work as stoppers and a concerning lack of rebounding will combine to keep the Jazz in the bottom five of defensive efficiency.

Last year's No. 29 ranking probably isn't repeatable as long as Jaren Jackson Jr. stays healthy, but Utah is going to have an extremely hard time cutting off penetration if Keyonte George and Darryn Peterson struggle on D as expected. From there, neither Jusuf Nurkić not Jaxson Hayes profile as reliable paint protectors.

Top that off with a cast of wing defenders that might be the worst in the league unless Ace Bailey takes a leap, and it's difficult to see where the Jazz can avoid being exploited.

The good news: Head coach Will Hardy's offense could be as potent as the defense is toothless. If Utah can score at a top-five rate, it'll stay in games all season and push for a win total in the low 40s.

Washington Wizards: Trae Young Can't Carry the Offense

In one sense, it might not be the worst thing if Trae Young isn't good enough to function as the be-all, end-all for the Washington Wizards' offense. That would mean other players, including younger options like AJ Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Tre Johnson and even Kyshawn George would get more time on the ball.

Overall, though, Young's likely failure as an offensive engine will be a massive problem.

Washington gave him a four-year, $213 million contract to run the show. That money will be very ill-spent if Young's preseason struggles drag deeper into the year. After a solid debut, he shot just 2-of-13 from deep and piled up 18 turnovers against 26 assists in his next three games.

Whether the Wizards succeed in getting some off-ball value from Young or not, errant shooting and a lack of ball control will do real damage to the whole operation. Young was once an offense unto himself. Now, it's possible he's not very helpful even if playing a smaller role.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: The Kristaps Porziņģis Trade Idea That Makes Most Sense for Golden State Warriors
articles.summary: Not to get all early-season-overreaction mode on everyone, but this already feels like red-alert time for the Golden State Warriors.
articles.body:
Not to get all early-season-overreaction mode on everyone, but this already feels like red-alert time for the Golden State Warriors.

Or, at least it does under the assumption they're aiming to give Stephen Curry the chance to play for something of significance before the curtains drop on his legendary career.

He needs help that the injury-ravaged Warriors are incapable of providing. Boxes for support scoring, shot-creation and competence at the center spot remain unchecked due to the myriad medical issues facing this team, namely the ACL recovery sidelining Jimmy Butler III into the new year and the autoimmune condition threatening to end Kristaps Porziņģis's career.

The first time the Warriors hit the hardwood this season, their second-leading scorer (reserve guard Brandon Williams) netted just 14 points—on 3-of-12 shooting. Things already appear strikingly bleak in the Bay.

They don't have to stay that way, though. Not with the Warriors working the trade market and having some interesting assets at their disposal. They may not find anyone available who's worth an all-in wager, but the following return could strike the right balance between risk and reward.

Golden State Warriors receive: Myles Turner and Ryan Rollins

Milwaukee Bucks receive: Kristaps Porziņģis, Moses Moody, 2028 first-round pick and 2031 first-round pick swap

I mean, did you see the season-opener? Curry couldn't get any kind of offensive support, and the undersized, Porziņģis-less Warriors offered zero resistance on the interior. The Los Angeles Lakers tallied 66 points and shot 56.8 percent from the field. Their starting center, Walker Kessler, had 26 points on a perfect 12-of-12 shooting.

"It's no secret that [center] spot was an important one for us, especially with [Porziņģis's] skill set," Curry told reporters afterward.

While Myles Turner has never hit the statistical highs of Porziņģis, the basic components of their skill sets are similar. Both fit the unicorn mold of shot-blocking, floor-spacing centers. Turner's 6'11", 250-pound frame alone would bulk up this collection of bigs, and he'd arrive as both a two-time blocks champion and a 38.9 percent three-point shooter over the past two seasons.

He should be readily available, too, since the 30-year-old is clearly not a timeline fit for the post-Giannis Antetokounmpo Bucks. And they'd surely love to get out from underneath the $83.6 million he's owed between now and 2029.

The Warriors have already reached out to the Bucks about a Porziņģis trade but couldn't get traction so far, per The Athletic's Sam Amick . That suggests Golden State hasn't put the right assets on the table, perhaps because it (reasonably) doesn't believe an overpaid Turner is worth it.

But Turner plus Ryan Rollins? That might be a different story.

Rollins, who started his NBA career as a lightly-used reserve with the Warriors, broke out in a big way last season. His stat sheet showed one personal-best after the next, including 17.3 points (on 47.2/40.6/79.6 shooting) and 5.6 assists (against 2.7 turnovers). Between the scoring punch, the on-ball craft and the off-ball shooting threat, he could give this group a lot of what it's missing next to Curry at the moment.

Bucks fans figure to be the hardest sell here, especially those who might be convinced they have a rising star in Rollins. Skepticism on that front is very much warranted, though, since all he has proven so far is the ability to post big(ish) numbers on a bad team.

Not to mention, this long-term backcourt could be just fine without him.

Tyler Herro, who's only 26, has a legitimate chance to star back in his home state, and Milwaukee has first-round guards from this year's draft (Brayden Burries, No. 10) and last year's (Kasparas Jakučionis, No. 20).

If nothing else, it would seem like a stretch for the Bucks to consider Rollins wholly off-limits given their need to stockpile assets for this top-to-bottom rebuild. And they'd walk with a healthy haul here, getting a 2028 first and a 2031 first-round swap from a team with an uncertain present and a wholly unprepared future.

Moody, 24, is more than a throw-in. He's out with a knee injury now, but there's no reason to doubt his ability to bounce all the way back—and maybe then some given his expected growth trajectory. At worst, he's a reliable 6'5" three-and-D swingman, and teams can never have too much of that archtype.

As for Porziņģis, he is simply around to make the money work, but the money works in Milwaukee's favor. After this season, he's owed just a $3 million guarantee on his $20 million salary for 2027-28.

Turner, on the other hand, will make $27.9 million and holds a $29.1 million player option for 2028-29 (his age-32 season). And Rollins will most certainly need a new deal next summer ( $4 million player option for next season), which Milwaukee may not be keen on covering given its backcourt depth.
